sections.title: The Significance of Wine
sections.html:
The wine that comes from grapes is a drink with special properties: it is both nourishing and gladdening, thanks to the alcohol in it. This is how the Holy One, blessed be He, created grapes: yeasts cling to their skins, and when the grapes are trodden and the grape skins are left with the liquid that came out of them, a fermentation is created by the yeasts that turns the sugars in the grape liquid into alcohol. Thus wine is created, with its deep and special taste and its gladdening alcohol. And this is the only fruit that naturally, without the need for professional knowledge and special equipment, if it is trodden and left to ferment, will turn into a nourishing drink containing alcohol. King David too, in the psalm of thanksgiving for the wonders of creation, mentioned gladdening wine, as it is stated (Tehillim 104:15): "And wine that gladdens the heart of man."

It is commonly thought, simplistically, that a righteous person who wishes to sanctify himself ought to be gloomy and sad, and to distance himself as far as possible from real life, so as not to be drawn after evil desires, frivolity and arrogance. However, according to the guidance of the Torah, holiness should be revealed in all areas of life, in spirit and in matter, in spiritual pleasure and in good taste. And not only does the satiating food necessary for a person's existence have value, but even gladdening wine.

And although every Jew is filled with spiritual delight when he cleaves to the Torah and the mitzvot, as long as the body does not share in the joy, not only is his body lacking, but even his spiritual joy is lacking. Therefore a person must be whole in his spirit and in his body, and when he rejoices over something positive that he has done, it is good that he involve his body in the joy. This is why the Sages instituted reciting a blessing over a cup of wine at every important occasion that has spiritual value, so that the spiritual joy will be accompanied by physical joy. Thus they instituted a cup of wine for betrothal and a cup of wine for marriage, a cup of wine for a brit mila and a cup of wine for pidyon ha-ben (redemption of the firstborn), a cup of wine for Kiddush of Shabbat and festivals and a cup of wine for Havdala. And even after a person dines in a group and thanks God in Birkat Ha-mazon, they instituted reciting a blessing over a cup of wine, so that the eating and the thanksgiving that flows from it will be in joy (above 5:13-15).

This is what the Sages said (Berakhot 35a): "Song is recited only over wine." Song is an expression of wholeness, and wholeness must necessarily include spirituality and physicality together (Ein Aya ibid.). And so it is said in the Zohar (vol. 3, 189b): "There is no sanctity except with wine, and there is no blessing except with wine."

The Torah too is likened to wine (Ta'anit 7a; Sifrei Devarim 11:22), for it too is meant to repair the entire world, in spirituality and in physicality, with pure truth and with vital joy. And Israel too, who were created to reveal the word of God in its fullness, are likened to a vine (Yeshayahu 5:1-7; Shemot Rabba 44:1).

Therefore, in the vow of a nazir not to drink wine there is a certain aspect of sin (Ta'anit 11a), for he deprives himself of physical joy that could contribute to his wholeness. And Rava said of himself that thanks to the wine he drank and the good fragrance he smelled, his mind was opened to novel Torah insights (see Yoma 76b).

sections.title: The Danger of Drunkenness
sections.html:
Every physical thing, when it accompanies spiritual values, not only does no harm but even benefits and helps reveal them. But when physicality becomes the main thing, it pushes aside spirituality and causes a person to become coarse and crude. All the more so with wine, which contains tremendous vitality expressing the ferment of physical life, and therefore its danger is especially great. One who becomes addicted to his desire for it and drinks it to excess becomes drunk and contemptible; his mind departs from him and the evil inclination rules over him. Therefore there are many severe warnings, in the Torah, the Prophets, the Writings and the words of our Sages, that a person should not drink wine excessively.

In the Torah we learned of Noaḥ and Lot, who fell and were disgraced because of drinking wine (Bereishit Rabba 36:4). And even the Tree of Knowledge through which Adam sinned was, according to Rabbi Meir, a vine, as the Sages said: "For there is nothing that brings wailing upon a person except wine" (Sanhedrin 70a). And regarding the sons of Aharon the Kohen too, they said that they died only because they entered the Mishkan having drunk wine (Vayikra Rabba 12:1).

In the books of the Prophets too we learned rebukes of those drawn after drinking wine, and even the exile was caused by the sin of wine (Bereishit Rabba 36:4). Regarding the Ten Tribes it is stated (Amos 6:6-7): "Who drink from bowls of wine and anoint themselves with the choicest oils, but are not grieved over the ruin of Yosef (and were not distressed by the prophecy of calamity). Therefore now they shall go into exile at the head of the exiles." And regarding the tribes of Yehuda and Binyamin it is stated (Yeshayahu 28:7): "These too reel with wine and stagger with strong drink."

Likewise we were warned in Mishlei (23:20-21): "Do not be among wine-guzzlers, among gluttonous eaters of meat. For the guzzler and the glutton will become impoverished (will become poor and destitute) …" And it is further stated (ibid. 29-30): "Who has woe, who has sorrow (who has screaming and wailing), who has strife, who has complaint, who has wounds without cause (who has quarrels, wounds and blows) … – those who linger over wine (who drink a lot until late), those who come to search out mixed wine" (who seek out good wine).

Likewise we find in the words of our Sages many warnings that wine may make a person poor and desolate and bring him to sin (see Sanhedrin 70a; Vayikra Rabba 12:5).

And they also said: "There is one who drinks wine and it is good for him, and there is one who drinks wine and it is bad for him. A Torah scholar drinks and it is good for him; an ignoramus (am ha-aretz) drinks and it is bad for him" (Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 4:6). For a Torah scholar knows how to drink in moderation, and then joy is added to him, and he grows stronger in the service of God, in spirituality and in physicality. And the Sages also said (Yoma 71a) that today, after the Temple was destroyed, "One who wishes to pour a libation upon the altar – let him fill the throats of Torah scholars with wine."

And wine is so dangerous that the true wine, good and strong, of the six days of Creation – the Holy One, blessed be He, hid away. And Israel, who laid down their lives in exile, and despite the tremendous difficulties continued to engage in the Torah that is sweeter than honey, and thereby showed that faith in God is the essence of their lives, and were ready to give their lives for it – them the Holy One, blessed be He, will in the future give to drink of the wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of Creation (Bamidbar Rabba 13:2).

Therefore the matter of wine is connected to a secret (sod) (see Eruvin 65a), for in its simple sense it may draw a person to sin, but when a person emphasizes the inner and spiritual, wine joins with holiness and reveals its good inner essence (Peninei Halakha: Zemanim 16:12). And in the future the secrets hidden in physical joy will be revealed in full, as stated in the Zohar Ha-ne'elam (vol. 1, 135b): "The wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of Creation – these are ancient matters that have not been revealed to man since the day the world was created, and they are destined to be revealed to the righteous in the World to Come."

sections.title: The Blessing over Wine
sections.html:
The most important drink for a person is wine, which nourishes and gladdens, and therefore the Sages instituted a special blessing for it – "Borei peri ha-gafen" ("who creates the fruit of the vine"). This is unlike orange juice, grapefruit juice and other fruit juices, which, since they have turned from fruit into a drink, have lost their stature as fruit, and over which one recites the most general blessing – Shehakol. And it is unlike grapes, over which one recites Ha-etz, which is the general blessing recited over all fruits of the tree. Over wine, which has been elevated from its previous state, the Sages instituted a special blessing – "Borei peri ha-gafen" – in order to add praise and thanksgiving to God for the gladdening wine.

One who drinks a revi'it of wine (75 ml), since it is one of the seven species, recites after it one Me'ein Shalosh blessing; however, since wine has been elevated from its state as grapes, instead of saying "for the tree and for the fruit of the tree" as one says over fruits of the seven species, including grapes, over wine one says: "for the vine and for the fruit of the vine."

Another law stems from the importance of wine: the Ha-motzi blessing over bread does not exempt it, and one who wishes to drink wine during a meal recites Ha-gafen over it. This is the difference between wine and other drinks, for all other drinks that a person drinks during a meal become secondary to the bread and are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing. But wine, even when drunk during a meal, because of its importance does not become secondary to the bread and is not exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing, and therefore one must recite Ha-gafen over it.

However, Birkat Ha-mazon after eating bread also exempts the wine drunk during the meal, because over wine one must recite one Me'ein Shalosh blessing, whereas Birkat Ha-mazon includes within it the three blessings themselves in full (SA 174, paragraphs 1, 6, 7).

sections.title: The Blessing over Wine Exempts Other Drinks
sections.html:
Just as bread is the head of all satiating foods, so wine is the head of all drinks. The uniqueness of wine is that it is also nourishing, because of the high sugar content of the fruit, which gives it caloric value, and in addition it gladdens, for the vitality it gives a person is accompanied by bodily joy.

Just as the Ha-motzi blessing over bread exempts the other foods of the meal (above 3:6), so the Ha-gafen blessing over wine exempts all drinks. This is on condition that those drinks are before him when he recites the blessing over the wine, or that he has in mind to drink them when he recites the blessing over the wine, or that he is accustomed to drink them at that time, in which case he exempts them even without having thought of them explicitly (SA 174:2).1

Likewise, participants in a Kiddusha Rabba (a Kiddush reception), which celebrants hold after the Musaf prayer of Shabbat, who heard the Kiddush and drank of the wine, need not recite a blessing over the other drinks, for they have already been exempted by the blessing over the wine.

Ideally, it is good that one drink of the wine a melo lugmav (a cheekful; about 50 ml, about a quarter of a regular cup), because some hold that only if he drinks this amount will the wine be considered primary and all the other drinks he intends to drink be secondary to it and exempted by its blessing (BHL 174:2). But in practice, even if one did not drink a cheekful, he may drink other beverages without a blessing, for this is the opinion of most poskim.2

One who heard the Kiddush and did not drink any of the wine, even though by hearing he fulfilled the obligation of Kiddush, the beverages he drinks do not become secondary to the wine, and he must recite Shehakol before them and Borei Nefashot after them.

One who drinks of the wine the amount that obligates an after-blessing (below 10:10) exempts the other drinks with the Me'ein Shalosh blessing he recites over the wine (SA 208:16). But if he did not drink of the wine the amount that obligates an after-blessing, while of the other drinks he drank the amount that obligates an after-blessing, he should recite Borei Nefashot over them (Seder Birkhot Ha-nehenin of the Gra"z 1:21).3

sections.title: Wine Diluted with Water
sections.html:
In the past, the taste of wines was harsh and strong, and they were not fit for drinking without dilution with water. The accepted dilution ratio was one quarter wine and three quarters water (Bava Batra 96b). And even if the wine was only one sixth of the mixture, as long as its taste was like the taste of wine, people would recite Ha-gafen over it, and after drinking a revi'it, Me'ein Shalosh. But if the proportion of wine was only one seventh, they recited Shehakol over it (Rema OḤ 204:5; YD 134:5). And some follow this practice to this day.

But according to several poskim, our wines are weaker, and only when the wine is the majority relative to the water does one recite Ha-gafen over it, and then the water too combines toward the amount of a revi'it for reciting Me'ein Shalosh.4

Since there are wineries in which water is mixed into sweet and inexpensive wines, one should be careful not to add a lot of water to simple sweet wines, lest through the addition of water the water become the majority relative to the wine, and according to many poskim one would not be able to recite Ha-gafen over it. But a little water that hardly changes the taste of the wine may be added to them as well.

sections.title: Cooked Wine and Grape Juice
sections.html:
Even if the wine was pasteurized or cooked, one recites Ha-gafen over it, for cooking does not change it.

Likewise, if sugar or honey or other flavorings were added to it, such as those customarily added to spiced wine (konditon), since the wine is the main component and they came to flavor it, its blessing is Ha-gafen (SA 202:1). Likewise, over vermouth that is drunk for pleasure one recites Ha-gafen, because its main component is wine, and the other spices are meant to flavor it (BHL ibid.).5

Likewise over grape juice, even though it does not intoxicate and gladden – since it is produced from the fruit of the vine like wine, it too merits the stature of wine, and one recites Ha-gafen over it (SA 202:1), and with its blessing all other drinks are exempted. And if water was added to the grape juice, as long as the water is a minority, its blessing is Ha-gafen and Al Ha-gefen.6

sections.title: The Ha-tov Ve-hametiv Blessing over Additional Wine
sections.html:
The Sages instituted a blessing over drinking additional wine: if people were drinking wine together, and afterwards they came to drink a different kind of wine, even though they already recited Ha-gafen over the first wine, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv ("who is good and does good") before drinking the additional wine. Likewise, if a third wine was brought to them, they should again recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it, and so they should recite it over each additional wine they drink. The intention of this blessing is to thank God for the abundance of wine.

This law is unique to wine, for if people were eating bread, and afterwards came to eat another kind of bread, they do not recite a special blessing over it; rather, with the blessing they recited over the first bread they exempted the second as well. The same is the law regarding different kinds of meat: they are all exempted with one blessing. Only over wine did the Sages institute a blessing for the abundance of its kinds, because it has a special quality: in addition to being satiating it also gladdens, and each wine has its own character, and when another kind of wine is drunk together, the joy increases; therefore they instituted reciting a blessing over the abundance of wine (Berakhot 59b; Tosafot and Rosh ibid.).

The second wine need not be superior to the first; rather, as long as it is not known to be inferior to the first, since it is different, it has some novelty in its taste or quality, and one recites Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it. Therefore, if there were several bottles of different wines before them, they should recite Ha-gafen over the first, and over each additional wine they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. And even if the two bottles were of one variety, if they were made in a different manner or are from a different vintage, such that there is a difference between them that is noticeable in taste to the drinkers, they should recite Ha-gafen over the first and Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over the second. And even if the second wine is cheaper than the first, as long as it has a certain advantage that the first lacks, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it (SA 175:2, 6).

If there were two wines before them, one good and the other clearly inferior to it, the law is that one must recite Ha-gafen over the good wine, as one must always recite the blessing over the superior kind. And since the second is entirely inferior to it, they can no longer recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it (SA 175:3; and see MB 14).7

sections.title: Conditions for the Blessing
sections.html:
One recites the Ha-tov Ve-hametiv blessing only when at least two people drink the second wine together, because there is no true joy in drinking that a person drinks alone. So too is implied by the wording of the blessing – "who is good and does good" – good to him and doing good to his fellow. Family members too, such as a husband and wife or a father and son, are considered two who drink together (SA 175:4).

As a rule, it is preferable that one person recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv on behalf of the other diners, for thereby the blessing is said with greater dignity. But if they are busy with their eating and do not pause to drink together, it is preferable that each one recite the blessing for himself (see SA 175:5, 6; 213:1; and below 12:7; 13:8).

If their first wine ran out and another wine was brought – one does not recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over the second, for there is not so much joy of abundance of wine in it, since it was brought because the first wine ran out (MB 175:3). However, it seems that if they have in the house another closed bottle of the same kind, if they open a wine of a different kind, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it.

If they had there a third wine that has some novelty in its taste or quality, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it too, and likewise over a fourth wine and onward. It is preferable that when they recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over the second wine, there not be on the table additional wines over which they wish to recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv afterwards, so that each time an additional wine is brought to the table the joy will be renewed, and as a result they will recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv.

If they recited Kiddush over grape juice, and afterwards during the meal drank wine, they recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it, for the first wine can be grape juice, but the second, gladdening wine must contain alcohol.

Some are very stringent in this law, taking all the opinions into account, so that it turns out that they almost never recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over wine; it is proper for them at least to contemplate the Ha-tov Ve-hametiv blessing in their hearts. However, in halakha, almost all the Aḥaronim ruled in practice that one recites Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over additional wine.8
